channel.title: Views From the On-Call Chair
channel.description: War stories, outages, and jargon translated for regular people.

item.title: The Config Push That Should Not Have Happened
item.description: Someone adding new devices to an automation tool accidentally aimed a live configuration push at production, and production noticed immediately.

item.title: Too Many Routes, Not Enough Limit
item.description: A network session dropped simply because it was told it could not possibly be receiving that many routes, even though it was.

item.title: The Tools That Cried Wolf
item.description: A quiet firmware bug took down a legacy router, and half our toolchain took it personally.

item.title: The Video Hiccup Heard Down South
item.description: A routine network change briefly took a few hundred live channels off the air, which is a fun way to find out how many live channels you actually have.

item.title: Four Strands of Glass
item.description: Business apps went quiet for nearly two hours because four glass strands between two buildings decided to stop cooperating at once.

item.title: The Load Balancers That Forgot How to Balance
item.description: The machines whose entire job is staying calm and distributing load instead crashed repeatedly for over a week.

item.title: The Clock That Needed a Very Specific Path
item.description: A network cleanup removed some links that looked redundant and unnecessary on paper, except one very picky protocol needed them specifically.

item.title: The Firewall Rule That Forgot Its Own Name
item.description: Renaming a label on a firewall rule quietly broke DNS for an entire site, because the rename did not take the way everyone assumed it had.

item.title: When Both Feeds Lean on the Same Crutch
item.description: A backup design meant to protect two independent live feeds turned out to secretly depend on the same single point of failure for both of them.

item.title: A Policy So Quiet It Fooled Everyone
item.description: A routine policy change silently stopped advertising a data center's own address space to the internet, and the immediate post change check somehow looked fine anyway.

item.title: The Night Both Wires Under the Ocean Went Quiet
item.description: Connectivity between two continents dropped because the backup path for an already broken cable picked the worst possible night for planned maintenance.

item.title: The Change That Was Not Supposed to Happen
item.description: While fixing one small, unrelated issue, someone made an edit that was never supposed to touch production, and production noticed fast.

item.title: The VPN That Picked a Fight With Itself
item.description: Remote access ground to a halt for an entire region, and it took two unrelated bugs colliding to do it.

item.title: The Certificate That Expired Quietly
item.description: An entire platform for on demand video stopped starting playback for everyone, because a security certificate simply ran out the clock.

item.title: The Limit Nobody Remembered Was There
item.description: Adding one new office network to the routing table was all it took to quietly exceed a limit set years earlier and drop every session on two routers at once.

item.title: The Day the Internet Forgot Who We Were
item.description: One fiber cut caused a failover that worked exactly as designed, and then a second problem, caused by the fix for the first one, took out a completely different region.

item.title: The Switch That Thought It Had a Partner
item.description: Two brand new switches were configured to work as a pair, except neither one actually had a partner, and the network layer that depends on that pairing quietly broke.

item.title: Two New Neighbors, Same Address
item.description: Two newly deployed switches were handed the exact same internal address as two switches that already existed, and everyone found out the hard way.

item.title: The Tool That Cleaned Up a Little Too Well
item.description: A routine sync of switch configurations wiped out settings nobody had told the syncing tool about in the first place.

item.title: The Multicast That Forgot to Say Please
item.description: A migration went smoothly right up until the new equipment tried to join a group conversation nobody had actually invited it to.

item.title: The Cable That Was Plugged In Wrong, on Paper
item.description: A same day router swap left a network connection configured just wrong enough to break playback for a national sports feed.

item.title: The Switch Swap That Remembered Too Much
item.description: A brand new replacement switch was handed a configuration from its own memory that nobody wanted it to remember.

item.title: Decommissioning Day Goes Sideways
item.description: Turning off equipment that was supposed to be safely retired quietly pulled the rug out from under the equipment that had replaced it.

item.title: The Address Two Devices Agreed to Share
item.description: An entire data center went unreachable because some new switches were handed addresses that already belonged to the devices in charge of getting traffic in and out.

item.title: The Buffer That Got Stuck
item.description: One single network port developed a very specific, very stubborn hardware problem that only affected traffic taking one particular path.

item.title: Two Cables, One Maintenance Window
item.description: A provider scheduled maintenance on both of a location's supposedly redundant circuits at the same time, which rather defeats the purpose of having two.

item.title: The Limit a Vendor Forgot to Mention
item.description: An internet provider quietly imposed a limit on how many routes it would accept from us, never told anyone, and then enforced it without warning.
